articles.title: Russia-Azerbaijan Economic Relations Shift Towards Investment, Trade Recovery and Regional Logistics - Modern Ghana
articles.summary: Russia-Azerbaijan Economic Relations Shift Towards Investment, Trade Recovery and Regional Logistics  Modern Ghana
articles.full_text:
The deterioration in trade follows several years of political and diplomatic friction, including the December 2024 Azerbaijani aircraft disaster, disagreements surrounding Karabakh and tensions following the detention of Azerbaijani diaspora members in Russia in 2025. Concerns about secondary sanctions and Azerbaijan’s efforts to diversify its strategic partnerships have added further complications. Nevertheless, bilateral trade totalled US$4.92 billion in 2025, an increase of 2.5% over 2024, demonstrating the underlying importance of the relationship. Russia was Azerbaijan’s third-largest foreign-trade partner, accounting for 9.96% of its total trade. The current decline therefore represents a significant commercial challenge, but not necessarily a permanent retreat from economic cooperation.
Agriculture remains one of the strongest foundations for maintaining trade flows. Russia purchased more than US$1.174 billion in Azerbaijani non-oil products in 2025, including agricultural exports exceeding US$837 million. Fruit and vegetable shipments alone reached US$696 million, supported by increasing demand for Azerbaijani produce. During early 2026, Russian imports of onions from Azerbaijan rose sharply, while strawberry, potato and pear shipments also recorded increases. Meanwhile, Russian agricultural supplies to Azerbaijan exceeded US$832 million, illustrating the reciprocal nature of agricultural trade. These established commercial relationships offer opportunities to stabilise bilateral turnover while political and administrative obstacles are addressed.
Investment developments present a more positive picture. Russian direct investment in Azerbaijan reached US$237.119 million in the first half of 2026, an increase of 82.8% from US$129.727 million during the corresponding period of 2025. Russia accounted for 6.5% of foreign direct investment entering Azerbaijan during the period. By contrast, Azerbaijani investment in Russia fell 20.6% to US$22.488 million. Accumulated Russian investment in Azerbaijan has been reported at approximately US$10.7 billion, including US$2.9 billion in the non-oil economy, while more than 1,400 Russian-capitalised companies were registered as active in Azerbaijan in April 2026. These businesses provide a foundation for expanding manufacturing, distribution, services and other commercial activities, although rising investment alone cannot compensate for declining merchandise trade.
The September and October diplomatic engagements reflect efforts to translate this economic foundation into practical results. On September 26, Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexander Novak met Azerbaijani Deputy Prime Minister Shahin Mustafayev in Baku to discuss industry, energy, transport and logistics. On October 5, Mustafayev and Russian Deputy Prime Minister Alexei Overchuk chaired intergovernmental discussions in Moscow, focusing on trade, investment, border-crossing capacity, freight transportation and the implementation of existing agreements. The October 9 meeting between Russian President Vladimir Putin, Azerbaijani President Ilham Aliyev and Iranian President Masoud Pezeshkian in Turkmenistan further highlighted the importance of regional economic coordination. Although these engagements did not establish a new quantified trilateral infrastructure package, they reinforced the political framework for cooperation.
The INSTC is central to this emerging agenda. Azerbaijan provides a strategic overland link between Russia and Iran, connecting northern markets with the Persian Gulf, India and wider South Asian destinations. Improving customs procedures, freight handling, railway operations and border-crossing efficiency could reduce transport costs and make the corridor more competitive. September 2026 freight traffic on the Russian-Azerbaijani border averaged approximately 840 cargo vehicles daily, while the reconstructed Yarag-Kazmalyar crossing reportedly increased potential border capacity from around 400 to 1,900 freight vehicles per day. However, infrastructure capacity must be matched by efficient administration, predictable transit times and commercially viable transport services.
Completing the approximately 160-kilometre Rasht-Astara railway section in Iran remains a major challenge for the corridor’s western route. The project has faced delays associated with land acquisition and administrative procedures, with completion targeted for 2030. Meanwhile, declining Caspian Sea water levels pose additional risks to maritime transport, port operations and regional logistics investment. Competing connectivity initiatives, including the proposed Trump Route for International Peace and Prosperity (TRIPP), also illustrate how geopolitical interests and infrastructure ownership are shaping the South Caucasus transport landscape.
As highlighted by Russia’s Pivot to Asia, the central question is whether renewed diplomatic engagement can generate measurable commercial improvements. Priorities include reversing the decline in Russian exports to Azerbaijan, sustaining Azerbaijani non-oil exports, converting investment into productive capacity and resolving transport bottlenecks. The relationship increasingly depends on three interconnected factors: established trade networks, expanding investment and Azerbaijan’s geographical position between Russia and Iran. The autumn meetings have established a framework for cooperation, but long-term success will depend on implementing existing commitments, completing critical infrastructure and restoring sustainable growth in bilateral trade.
Zaur Safarov
Eurasian Market Analyst & Consultant
Market Policy
Baku, Azerbaijan

Toplines
Ukrainian officials are widely reporting continued in-motion speed restrictions on SpaceX’s low-earth orbit satellite communication technology (Starlink and Starshield) on October 23, but the situation remains unclear. Ukrainian sources, including the Ukrainian General Staff and sources within the Ukrainian Ministry of Defense (MoD), reported on October 23 that Ukrainian forces have observed “cases of connection loss” in Starlink/Starshield terminal operations at speeds of 161 kilometers per hour (around 100 miles per hour).[1] Sources within the Ukrainian MoD stated that there has been “no confirmation” about the removal of in-motion speed restrictions.[2] Former adviser to the Ukrainian defense minister Serhii Sternenko stated that the situation with Starlink/Starshield speed restrictions “remains ambiguous” since some Ukrainian units report the resumption of operations at speeds exceeding the previously established limits, but the resumption does not apply to all missions, and he noted that some disruptions continue.[3] The situation regarding in-motion Starlink/Starshield speed restrictions remains unclear, but Ukrainian sources are emphasizing that Ukrainian forces continue experiencing problems with accessing Starlink/Starshield terminals as of October 23.
Russia and Ukraine have reportedly agreed to a limited ceasefire in Russian-occupied Oleshky, Kherson Oblast. The White House reported on October 23 that US First Lady Melania Trump secured a localized ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in Russia-occupied Oleshky, Kherson Oblast beginning on October 29 to facilitate humanitarian aid deliveries and a civilian evacuation from the city amid a dire humanitarian crisis.[4] Ukraine’s Human Rights Commissioner Dmytro Lubinets confirmed on October 23 the White House’s press release and noted that Ukraine and Russia agreed to conduct a humanitarian mission in occupied Oleshky, including securing a limited ceasefire, delivering humanitarian cargo to the city, and ensuring the free movement of civilians from the settlement.[5] Russian Chief of the General Staff Army General Valery Gerasimov confirmed on October 23 that Russia agreed to the limited ceasefire in the Kherson direction beginning at 0400 local Moscow time on October 27 — a notably different start date from the one given in the White House press release.[6]
Russian occupation authorities are fully responsible for the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky and have repeatedly and deliberately blocked evacuation and humanitarian routes into the settlement since the beginning of Russia’s occupation.[7] Russian occupation authorities stopped the delivery of food and other critical supplies into Oleshky in late December 2025 and have failed to deliver any food or medicine to Oleshky since May 2026. The Kremlin rejected three local humanitarian ceasefire proposals from Ukrainian Ombudsman Dmytro Lubinets in May, July, and September 2026, after which Ukrainian forces conducted an operation to provide food to Oleshky residents via drone drops in September 2026.[8] Russian authorities have long refused to address the humanitarian crisis in Oleshky, and Gerasimov’s October 23 statement is the first instance of a Russian attempt to facilitate humanitarian aid deliveries.
Russian President Vladimir Putin articulated his long-standing commitment to wider territorial aims in Ukraine far beyond Donetsk Oblast by invoking mythologized and false Russian “historical claims”.
Putin claimed on October 22 that occupied Ukraine is “the territory of historical Russia” while rejecting Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelensky’s October 21 proposal to freeze the current frontline as part of a ceasefire agreement.
[9] Putin also claimed that the “latest genetic research” identifies Russians and Ukrainians as “one people.
” Putin’s October 22 reference to “historical Russia” likely refers to “Novorossiya” — an amorphous invented region in southern and eastern Ukraine that the Kremlin has claimed is “integral” to Russia.
[10] Novorossiya notably includes not only Crimea and the four oblasts that Russia has illegally annexed (Luhansk, Donetsk, Zaporizhia, and Kherson oblasts), but also Kharkiv, Dnipropetrovsk, Mykolaiv, and Odesa oblasts.
[11] Putin’s invocation of Russia’s historical claims demands that Ukraine surrender the Ukrainian-controlled 20.
5 percent of Donetsk Oblast, 24.
5 percent of Zaporizhia Oblast, including Zaporizhzhia City with a pre-war population of over 700,000 people, and 30 percent of Kherson Oblast, including Kherson City with a pre-war population of nearly 300,000 people.
Putin’s October 23 statement explicitly demonstrates that Russian demands extend far beyond Ukraine’s Fortress Belt and Donetsk Oblast and may include the entire territory of Ukraine.
Putin also emphasized his commitment to achieving all Russian war goals, which include the Russian demand for Ukraine’s full capitulation.
[12] Putin’s statement demonstrates that the Kremlin is willing to participate in “negotiations” with Ukraine solely for the purpose of accepting Kyiv’s surrender — not for the purpose of coming to some compromise peace agreement.

Putin also agreed to discuss the “European security architecture as a whole” after ensuring Ukraine’s and Russia’s future security.[13] Putin’s comment on “revising” the European security architecture refers to another Russian long-standing demand first articulated in the December 2021 ultimatum preceding the full-scale invasion that includes halting the deployment of military forces and weapons systems to NATO states that joined the alliance after 1997 and granting Russia a veto over certain NATO exercises.[14] Putin’s December 2021 demands are incompatible with US President Donald Trump’s commitment to maintaining a US military presence in Poland and the current US troop deployments in the Baltic States.
The Kremlin appears to be increasingly adopting a more cautious monetary policy amid continued inflationary pressures, which may pose risks to wage growth and Russia’s defense industrial base (DIB).
The Russian Central Bank announced on October 23 that it would keep the key interest rate at 14 percent for the second consecutive month, after lowering the rate 10 times over the past 18 months, citing elevated price pressure and high inflation expectations.
[15] The Central Bank’s baseline scenario assumes an average key interest rate of 12.
5 to 13.
5 percent in 2027 — only 0.
5 to 1.
5 percentage points below the current rate.
The Central Bank noted that underlying price growth is “not slowing” and identified pro-inflationary risks (or risk factors that increase inflation over the medium term), including price growth between five and six percent and estimated annual inflation of 6.
8 percent.
The Central Bank estimated that annual inflation will range between 7.
1 and 7.
6 percent by the end of 2026, a slight increase from the Central Bank’s September 11 announcement, and noted that volatile items like motor fuel (an oblique reference to the effects of Ukrainian strikes on Russian energy infrastructure) will continue impacting price dynamics.
Russian Central Bank Chairwoman Elvira Nabiullina stated on October 23 that supply and demand continue facing inflationary risks, elevated inflation expectations, labor market tensions, and a larger budget deficit.
[16] Nabiullina stated that Russia has experienced a decrease in consumer activity and that Russia’s GDP growth estimates for 2026 are between 0.
5 and one percent.
Nabiullina stated that the Central Bank is aiming to return the inflation rate to four percent in 2027.

The Russian Central Bank’s continued reduction of the key interest rate over an 18-month period prior to September 2026 likely contributed to domestic inflationary pressures.[17] Nabiullina has consistently expressed the need for monetary restraint — often trying to resist the Kremlin’s demands to expand capital availability for the Russian DIB and devalue the ruble to increase export revenues, despite ongoing fiscal inflationary pressures.[18] The Central Bank’s apparent success in avoiding further interest rate reductions at this time indicates that Putin has likely become more tolerant of contractionary monetary policy. Putin has recently prioritized reducing inflation to secure support amongst the Russian population by attempting to reduce the economic effects of Russian war spending, a prioritization that may have led him to accept Nabiullina’s fiscal policy for now.[19] Keeping the key rate at the current level will likely suppress wage growth and limit the amount of capital available to the Russian DIB, which may prevent Putin from achieving his goals of raising Russians’ effective purchasing power and maintaining the DIB’s production capacity. It remains difficult to assess, however, what effect fiscal policy will have on wage inflation and Russians’ quality of life, since Russia’s persistent labor shortages drive wage inflation for employed individuals while households face pressures that nominal wage figures do not capture.[20]
A likely Russian drone struck a cargo ship off the coast of Romania and drone debris fell in Moldova on October 23.
Romanian President Nicusor Dan stated on October 23 that an unspecified drone struck a Comoros-flagged Khoryv cargo ship “near Romanian territorial waters” and added that the strike is a consequence of “Russia’s aggression against Ukraine.
”[21] The Romanian Naval Authority reported that the Khoryv vessel sent a distress signal about 13 nautical miles (around 24 kilometers and just outside of the Romanian territorial waters) off the coast of Constanta, Romania.
[22] European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen called the October 23 drone strike yet another “Russian escalation” in the Black Sea.
[23] Territorial waters extend up to 12 nautical miles (about 22 kilometers) from the country’s shoreline, and states have sovereignty and jurisdiction over their territorial waters.
